references.text: Passover as a memorial feast. The Lord commanded Israel to celebrate Passover as a day of remembrance: "This day shall be a memorial for you" (Exod 12:14). Jesus' words "do this in memory of me" link the Lord's Supper directly to the Passover meal and the idea of a repeated act of remembrance.

Moses took the blood and sprinkled it on the people, saying, "See, this is the blood of the covenant" (Exod 24:8). Jesus' words "this is my body" and the institution of the new covenant recall the making of the Sinai covenant with blood.
Matthew's parallel account of the institution of the Lord's Supper: Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, "This is my body" (Matt 26:26-28).
Mark's parallel account of the institution of the Lord's Supper. Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, "This is my body" (Mark 14:22-24).
The immediate context: Jesus sits down at the table with the apostles for the Passover meal and expresses his deep desire to celebrate this meal with them before his suffering (Luke 22:14-18).

Jesus calls himself the bread of life and says, "The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world" (John 6:51-56). The expression "my body given for you" in Luke 22:19 has a close thematic parallel to Jesus' speech about giving his flesh for the life of the world.

Paul links the breaking of bread to fellowship with the body of Christ: "The bread that we break, does it not share in the body of Christ?" (1 Cor 10:16-17). The Lord's Supper as participation in the body of Christ.

Paul's account of the words instituting the Lord's Supper, which is very close to Luke's version: "This is my body, which is for you. Do this in memory of me!" (1 Cor 11:23-25). The clearest parallel to Luke 22:19, with the same expression "in memory of me" (εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν).

"By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all" (Heb 10:10). Jesus' body given for us as a final sacrifice, which the words of the Lord's Supper "given for you" point forward to.

The suffering servant of the Lord "poured out his soul to death" and "bore the sin of many" (Isa 53:12). Jesus' words about the body that is "given for you" reflect the substitutionary suffering prophesied by Isaiah.
